claims.text: Selective chemical dealloying of a multicomponent high-entropy alloy precursor can produce three-dimensional nanoframeworks enriched in noble metals.
The proposed precursor is a dense high-entropy alloy containing noble metals and more reactive elements.
The precursor has a random solid-solution structure.
Acid or alkaline chemical etching can selectively dissolve the more reactive elements from the precursor.
Controlled temperature and etchant concentration can favor selective removal without collapse of the remaining structure.
An inert atmosphere may prevent unwanted side reactions during dealloying.
Selective removal of reactive elements creates interconnected pores and channels.
The interconnected pores and channels form a bicontinuous nanoframework.
Preferential dissolution of less noble elements causes the remaining noble-metal atoms to reorganize into a three-dimensional porous network.
The resulting porous network has high surface area that is beneficial for catalysis.
Dealloying will produce a three-dimensional nanoframework with enhanced active surface area.
Noble-metal sites will be uniformly distributed in the resulting nanoframework.
The nanoframework may exhibit improved catalytic performance relative to the unrestructured precursor.
The untreated precursor is dense and relatively nonporous, with limited accessible active sites.
Successful framework formation depends on alloy composition and dealloying conditions.
Overly aggressive etching or inappropriate precursor compositions may cause collapse or coarsening of the nanostructure.
